dmm-2014-team-02.title: Components of the divisibility graph
dmm-2014-team-02.body:
Numbers with a common divisor in the set get the same color, so a color class is a connected component of the graph joining each number to its divisors. Every number is joined to a prime factor. Any prime $p\le 50$ is joined to $2p\le100$, which is joined to $2$; so all primes up to $50$ (and everything divisible by them) lie in one component. The primes $53,59,61,67,71,73,79,83,89,97$ have no multiple other than themselves in the set, so each is isolated.

The number of colors is therefore $1+10=11$.

**Answer: 11**

dmm-2014-team-03.title: Inclusion-exclusion
dmm-2014-team-03.body:
We count ordered triples $(x,y,z)$ of distinct positive integers with $x+y+z=24$ (each is at most $22<100$). All positive triples: $\binom{23}{2}=253$. Triples with $x=y$: $z=24-2x\ge1$ gives $x=1,\dots,11$: $11$ triples; same for $y=z$ and $x=z$. The triple $(8,8,8)$ is counted in all three. So the number with some equality is $3\cdot11-3\cdot1+1=31$, and the answer is $253-31=222$.

**Answer: 222**

dmm-2014-team-04.title: Factor out 9
dmm-2014-team-04.body:
$\overline{abcd}-\overline{dcba}=999(a-d)+90(b-c)=9\,[111(a-d)-10(c-b)]$. With $u=a-d$ and $w=c-b$ ($w\ge1$ since $b<c$; $u\ge1$ so that the difference is positive), the bracket $111u-10w$ must be a perfect square. Its last digit is the last digit of $u$ (as $10w$ ends in $0$), and squares end in $0,1,4,5,6,9$, so $u\in\{1,4,5,6,9\}$; $u\le8$. Checking $u=4,5,6$: $444-10w\in[364,434]$ has no square ending in $4$; $555-10w\in[475,545]$ has no square ending in $5$; $666-10w\in[586,656]$ has no square ending in $6$. For $u=1$: $111-10w\in\{101,91,81,\dots\}$ is a square only for $81$ ($w=3$).

So the difference is $9\cdot81=729=27^2$ (e.g. $a-d=1,\ c-b=3$ as in $2141-1412=729$).

**Answer: 729**

dmm-2014-team-05.title: Bound each gap
dmm-2014-team-05.body:
The $34$ boxes $1,4,\dots,100$ hold $301$ balls. The remaining boxes form $33$ gaps of two consecutive boxes $(3k+2,3k+3)$. In each gap the two counts differ by $1$ and are at most $10$, so they cannot both be $10$ and their sum is at most $10+9=19$. Hence the total is at most $301+33\cdot19=928$.

This is attained: pick the selected counts alternating $9,x_1,9,x_2,\dots$ with each $x_i\in\{8,10\}$ (box $1$ has $x_1$). The gap between $9$ and $10$ can be filled $10,9$ (i.e. $9,10,9,10$) and between $10$ and $9$ as $9,10$, between $9$ and $8$ as $10,9$ and between $8$ and $9$ as $9,10$, so every gap sums to $19$ and consecutive boxes differ by $1$. The $17$ nines give $153$, so the $17$ values $x_i$ must sum to $148$: eleven $8$'s and six $10$'s. Hence $928$ is attained.

**Answer: 928**

dmm-2014-team-06.title: Power of a point
dmm-2014-team-06.body:
$A$ lies on line $DX$, so by the power of $A$ with respect to $\Gamma$: $AD\cdot AX=AP^2=36$. Since $\angle BAD=\angle XAC$ and $\angle ABD=\angle AXC$ (both subtend arc $AC$), triangles $ABD$ and $AXC$ are similar, so $\frac{AB}{AX}=\frac{AD}{AC}$, i.e. $AB\cdot AC=AD\cdot AX=36$. Hence $AC=\frac{36}{4}=9$.

**Answer: 9**

dmm-2014-team-07.title: Count degrees of red vertices
dmm-2014-team-07.body:
There are $2\cdot15\cdot16=480$ unit sides. A corner vertex lies on $2$ sides, a vertex on a side of the big square (not a corner) on $3$, an interior vertex on $4$. The red vertices: $2$ corners, $32$ side vertices and $133-34=99$ interior vertices, so they have $2\cdot2+32\cdot3+99\cdot4=496$ side-ends in total. Each red side has two red ends and each green side has one, so $2\,\#\text{red}+196=496$ and $\#\text{red}=150$. Hence $\#\text{blue}=480-150-196=134$.

(Check with the blue vertices: $2$ corners, $24$ side vertices, $97$ interior: $4+72+388=464=2\cdot134+196$.)

**Answer: 134**

dmm-2014-team-08.title: Inequalities on the total
dmm-2014-team-08.body:
Let $S$ be the total and $M$ the biggest pile. Redistributing a pile that is not the biggest leaves the biggest pile among the other nine, which must all end equal to $S/9$, so $M\le S/9$, i.e. $S\ge9M$. The piles are distinct, so $S\le M+(M-1)+\dots+(M-9)=10M-45$. Hence $9M\le10M-45$ and $M\ge45$.

For $M=45$ take the piles $36,37,\dots,45$: $S=405=9\cdot45$. Removing any pile and sharing it out brings the other nine up to $45$ each, using exactly $45\cdot9-(405-p)=p$ rocks. So the minimum is $45$.

**Answer: 45**

dmm-2014-team-09.title: Sum over Tony's number
dmm-2014-team-09.body:
Tony picks $i$ with probability $\frac i{21}$ and Danny picks $j$ with probability $\frac j{28}$. $P(\text{Tony}>\text{Danny})=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\frac i{21}\cdot\frac{1+2+\dots+(i-1)}{28}=\frac1{21\cdot56}\sum_{i=1}^6 i^2(i-1)=\frac{0+4+18+48+100+180}{1176}=\frac{350}{1176}=\frac{25}{84}$.

**Answer: $\frac{25}{84}$**

dmm-2014-team-10.title: Parity and bounds
dmm-2014-team-10.body:
A step never increases the total (the least prime factor of $s$ is at most $s$), so $\frac{n(n+1)}2\ge101$ and $n\ge14$. Track the parity: odd+even gives an odd number or an odd prime, odd+odd gives $2$, even+even gives $2$ (an even sum has least prime factor $2$). Each step reduces the number of odd numbers by $0$ or $2$, and we end with one odd number, so the number of odd numbers in $1,\dots,n$ must be odd. That rules out $n=15,16$.

The last step must combine $x,y$ with $x+y$ having least prime factor $101$, so $x+y=101$ (at most one even summand, equal to $2$ or an untouched even original). For $n=14$ and $n=17$ an exhaustive search of all merge orders finds no way to reach $101$ (for $n=17$ the only candidates are an untouched $4$ with $97$, or an untouched $12$ with $89$).

For $n=18$ the following merges work (each pair is replaced by the least prime factor of its sum): $(1,2)\to3$, $(3,3)\to2$, $(2,4)\to2$, $(2,5)\to7$, $(7,7)\to2$, $(2,9)\to11$, $(8,15)\to23$, $(6,23)\to29$, $(11,11)\to2$, $(2,13)\to3$, $(3,17)\to2$, $(2,29)\to31$, $(10,31)\to41$, $(12,41)\to53$, $(14,53)\to67$, $(16,67)\to83$, $(18,83)\to101$.

**Answer: 18**
